questions.q: The Court's list of top producers names Château Lafleur and Clos l'Église. In which Bordeaux appellation are their vineyards?
questions.exp: The Court lists Pétrus, Lafleur, Le Pin and Clos l'Église as Pomerol's top producers, all Merlot-led reds from the clay and gravel of the plateau. Pomerol has never been classified, so these names carry the appellation's reputation on their own; Saint-Émilion's top estates (Angélus, Ausone, Cheval Blanc, Pavie, Figeac) sit in its own classification.

questions.q: All three Léoville estates, Las Cases, Poyferré and Barton, are Second Growths of 1855. Which commune holds them?
questions.exp: The great Léoville estate was divided in the decades after the Revolution into Las Cases, Poyferré and Barton, and all three sit in Saint-Julien beside Ducru-Beaucaillou and Gruaud Larose, the commune's other Second Growths. The Court asks a Certified candidate to know the fourteen Second Growths with their communes.

questions.q: The Court sets two harmful rots against the noble rot of Sauternes. One is grey rot; name the other, a fungus that turns the berries into hard, shrivelled mummies.
questions.exp: Black rot is a fungal disease that spots the leaves and then turns the berries brown, black and shrivelled, and it thrives in the warm, wet springs a maritime climate brings. Grey rot is the destructive form of Botrytis cinerea, the fungus whose benign form, noble rot, makes Sauternes; the Bordeaux mixture of copper sulphate and lime was devised against downy mildew in the same damp conditions.

questions.q: A table orders Arcachon oysters and wants to stay in Bordeaux. Which appellation gives the crisp, unoaked, Sauvignon-led white the dish calls for?
questions.exp: Entre-Deux-Mers dry white, mostly Sauvignon Blanc with Sémillon and Muscadelle and made in steel, has the acidity and brisk citrus to cut the brine of an oyster; the appellation has also covered red since the 2023 vintage. Pessac-Léognan's barrel-fermented whites suit lobster and richer fish, Sauternes goes with foie gras and blue cheese, and Lalande-de-Pomerol is a red.

questions.q: Which river runs past the vineyards of Graves, Barsac and Sauternes on its way down to the city of Bordeaux?
questions.exp: The Garonne flows up from the Pyrenees past Sauternes, Barsac and the Graves to the city, then meets the Dordogne at the Bec d'Ambès to form the Gironde estuary. Its cool tributary, the Ciron, brings the autumn mists that breed noble rot; the Dordogne serves the Right Bank, the Isle joins it at Libourne and the Charente is Cognac's river.

questions.q: A bottle labelled Barsac AOP holds which style of wine?
questions.exp: Barsac is one of the five Sauternes communes and the only one that may use an appellation of its own, always for botrytised sweet white from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle. Its growers may label the wine Barsac or Sauternes, and a dry white from the same vines sells as Bordeaux Blanc.

questions.q: A guest asks why you are decanting a two-year-old Margaux that has thrown no deposit at all. In one word, what is that decant for?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified cell asks for both decants: a young, tannic Bordeaux is decanted for aeration, so that air opens its closed fruit and softens its grip, while an aged bottle is decanted slowly over a light to leave its sediment behind. A full red Bordeaux is served at about 16 to 18 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: Why did the brokers of 1855 rank Haut-Brion, a Graves estate, beside the three Médoc First Growths?
opts: Graves lay in the Médoc then
questions.exp: The 1855 list ranked estates by the prices their wines had fetched over many years, and Haut-Brion's prices stood level with those of Lafite, Latour and Margaux, so the brokers included it although it lies in the Graves; Mouton joined the first rank only in 1973. It is the only red outside the Médoc on the list, and it also tops the Classification of Graves of 1959.
